prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not give loperamide aggressively in cirrhosis (constipation precipitates HE) — manage diarrhea via sorafenib dose adjustment instead.
required_recommendations: Aggressive IV potassium and magnesium repletion (cardiac monitoring during K repletion).
Volume resuscitation with albumin to reverse pre-renal AKI.
Lactulose titrated to 2-4 soft stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BID.
Discuss sorafenib hold vs dose-reduction with oncology pending HE resolution.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), alcoholic cirrhosis with HCC on sorafenib (Child-Pugh B, MELD 16) — precipitated by sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing hypokalemia (K 2.8), hypomagnesemia, dehydration, and pre-renal AKI; concurrent low-grade fever requires SBP exclusion.

differential.key_features: Rare but reported sorafenib encephalopathy; would not produce asterixis or rapid lactulose response.
HCC rarely metastasizes to brain; would expect focal deficits and consider MRI if course atypical.
AKI is mostly pre-renal from diarrhea-related volume loss; reassess after fluid resuscitation.
Dehydration is a precipitant of HE in this patient, not a sole cause given cirrhosis and ammonia elevation.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Targeted therapies (sorafenib) commonly cause diarrhea; the electrolyte/volume consequences are a frequent HE precipitant in HCC patients on these drugs.
Fever in a cirrhotic with ascites is SBP until proven otherwise — paracentesis mandatory.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The sorafenib-related issue here is diarrhea → electrolyte loss → HE; direct CNS toxicity is rare.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute encephalopathy to HCC progression or 'sorafenib brain toxicity' and order extensive oncologic imaging.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mandatory paracentesis to exclude SBP; targeted empiric therapy only when ascitic PMN ≥250 or strong other source.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Default to broad-spectrum antibiotics without source workup.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma receiving sorafenib, presenting with a 1-week history of progressive confusion, word-finding difficulty, and behavioral change. His wife described increasing irritability, repeated conversations, and inability to balance his finances — activities he normally handles. He denies hematemesis or melena. He reports worsening nausea and diarrhea over the prior 3 weeks that his oncologist attributed to sorafenib side effects (sorafenib commonly causes diarrhea and nausea). His sorafenib dose has not been adjusted despite the diarrhea, which has been 3-5 watery stools per day. He has low-grade fever 38.2°C on admission.
